Subject: Pegasus Health — TTFT pacing check-in & SSE fallback plan

Hi Natalie — thanks again for the product + infra deep-dive earlier. Quick follow-up from our side with the items we discussed and the concrete asks so we can scope a pilot: 

Summary of requirements you mentioned
- Peak concurrent inference: ~120 concurrent sessions during business hours, up to 5k tokens/response on long summaries.
- Latency target (TTFT): 150–200 ms 95th for short prompts; 300–400 ms 95th for long summaries with streaming.
- Preferred streaming transport: SSE for web clients, but ops asked whether WS fallback is required for legacy mobile clients.
- Chunk cadence: preference for initial chunk within 200 ms, then subsequent chunks every 100–200 ms for progressive output.

Requests / next steps
1) Can you confirm whether the 120 concurrent sessions is steady-state or bursty (e.g., 120 sustained vs 250 for 30s bursts)? If bursty, please indicate burst windows.
2) Please attach the latency spreadsheet you mentioned (I referenced a placeholder). I attached our short checklist and the call recording for internal tech review.
3) Ops: can you confirm whether SSE is allowed through your CDN and whether you have any sticky session / websocket termination constraints?

We can put together a two-week pilot profile: baseline probes (synthetic TTFT probes), a small pilot with 10% production traffic routed through Redwood Dedicated, and a fallback policy (SSE primary, WS as fallback) with explicit chunk pacing. If that sounds right I’ll loop in Marissa and Ben to scope the runbook and an SLO matrix.

Thanks — I’ll be available all afternoon for any quick follow-ups.

— Karthik

Hi Karthik — thanks for the concise recap and for the recording. Quick clarifications: 

- Concurrency: 120 is our typical steady-state for our web app; we do see short bursts up to ~300 for up to 30–45s when a batch job kicks off (daily reports). So we need to be resilient to short bursts.
- TTFT: target is 95th <= 250 ms for short prompts (customer flows). For long summaries we’re comfortable with 400–500 ms 95th if overall UX is progressive (first token + streaming cadence matters more).
- SSE: our CDN supports SSE but there are proxy timeouts on some internal partner endpoints. Web clients are fine; mobile SDKs sometimes prefer WS. Ideally SSE primary with WS fallback for mobile.

I attached the latency spreadsheet (pegasus_latency_requirements.xlsx). Internal ops will follow up separately but @ops+infra: please confirm if there are any websocket termination limits on your edge.

Thanks — Natalie

Ack. Quick plan and assumptions from solutions: 

1) Synthetic probe profile
- I’ll produce two probe buckets: steady-state 120 conc at 1 request/s each and burst profile with 300 conc for 45s every hour. Probes will include short (<=64 token) and long (>=1k token) prompt templates to exercise KV cache and batching.

2) Expected numbers (rough preliminary)
- With our m-cpu64 quantized variant and continuous batching tuned to 8–12 ms batching window, we expect short TTFT 95th in ~180–260 ms range at steady-state. Bursts will increase 95th to ~320–450 ms unless we enable burst autoscaling to add an extra pool.

3) Chunk cadence and transport
- We'll default to SSE with a WS fallback. Implementation notes: SSE via CDN requires keepalive/ping headers to avoid proxy timeouts; we’ll include a 15s ping. For mobile WS fallback we’ll provide a websocket handshake endpoint and an explicit fallback header.

4) Pilot runbook highlights
- Canary 10% traffic for 48 hours, synthetic probes running in parallel.
- Autoscale policy: add 30% capacity at 90th usage threshold; full burst pool engagement above 200 concurrent sessions.
- SLO proposal to share with Natalie: Short prompts 95th <= 250 ms; Long progressive responses 95th <= 500 ms (with progressive-first-token <= 300 ms).

I’ll create the runbook doc in Drive and send the link; Ben — ping me when the probe harness is ready so I can embed sample graphs.

— Marissa
